The Path to the Majority
British Columbia · A strategist's map of the 2024 result

British Columbia · After the 2024 Election

The Path to
the Majority

The BC NDP governs on the narrowest possible margin — 47 of 93 seats. That majority does not rest on the party's strongholds. It rests on a thin band of suburbs, and on a few thousand votes. Here is the board, read from the NDP's side of the table.

An interactive briefing · Data: Elections BC official results (2013–2024) & Statistics Canada · All 2024 figures are actual counts

↓ Scroll to begin

01 · The boardEight regions, three postures

Group the 93 ridings into the regions that actually behave alike, and British Columbia resolves into three kinds of ground. Two blocs are banked for the NDP — Vancouver Island and the city of Vancouver. Three are a Conservative wall — the Interior, the North, and the Fraser Valley. Between them sits the only ground that is truly in play: the suburban Lower Mainland.

The colours below group seats by region and posture. The whole story is how few seats are actually contested — and where they are.

02 · The banked seats, IVancouver Island & the Coast

13NDP of 16
1Green
2Conservative

The Island is the NDP's oldest fortress. Sixteen seats, thirteen orange — the only gaps are a Conservative pair up-Island (Courtenay-Comox and North Island) and the Greens' seat in Saanich North and the Islands. The party's vote share here has sat near the mid-40s for a decade, with the Greens, not the Conservatives, as the only real competition for the left.

03 · The banked seats, IIThe city of Vancouver

11NDP of 12
1Conservative

Inside the city limits the NDP holds eleven of twelve — everything but wealthy Vancouver-Quilchena. And unlike the Island, the core is getting safer: the NDP's share of the vote here has climbed every election since 2013, from the high-40s to the high-50s. This is the bank vault.

04 · The wall, IThe Interior and the North

21Con of 25
4NDP holds

East of the Coast Mountains and up past Prince George, the map turns blue and stays blue. Of 25 Interior and Northern seats the Conservatives take 21; the NDP's survivors are a handful of north-coast and Kootenay holds. This wall is deep and, in the North, it is growing: NDP support there has slid from the mid-30s to 27 per cent.

05 · The wall, IIThe Fraser Valley

8Con of 8
0NDP holds

The Valley is the newer face of the wall — Langley, Abbotsford, Chilliwack, Mission — and the most complete: a Conservative sweep, eight for eight. The NDP actually gained ground here over the decade, lifting its share from the high-20s to about 40 per cent. It still wasn't close. This is the Conservatives' suburban anchor, and it holds.

06 · The hingeThe North Shore & Sea-to-Sky

2NDP of 4
1Green
1Conservative

Four seats across the water in West and North Vancouver and up to Whistler — small, affluent, and genuinely mixed. The NDP takes two, the Conservatives one, and one of the Greens' two seats sits here, in West Vancouver-Sea to Sky. Not a battleground that decides government, but a hinge worth watching.

07 · The battlegroundThe suburban Lower Mainland

17NDP of 28
11Conservative

Here is where the government is chosen. Twenty-eight seats across Surrey, Burnaby, the Tri-Cities, Richmond, Delta and Maple Ridge — more than a quarter of the entire legislature, and the only large bloc neither side can bank. The NDP took seventeen of them. It needed nearly all of them.

Watch the trend line: the NDP's suburban vote share surged to 55 per cent in the 2020 landslide, then fell back to 49 in 2024. That six-point give-back is the whole election.

08 · Below the riding lineEvery neighbourhood in British Columbia

Now drop beneath all 93 ridings. Each patch is a voting area — nearly 5,800 of them — shaded by the NDP's share at the election-day voting place that served it. Across the province the texture is unmistakable: deep orange through Vancouver and the Island towns, paler and bluer over the Interior, the North and the Fraser Valley. And in the suburban battleground the patchwork is tightest — NDP and Conservative ground interleaved almost block by block.

45.0Con · election-day %
42.9NDP · election-day %

A crucial caveat — and a story in itself: on election day the Conservatives actually led the province, 45.0 to 42.9. The NDP's 44.9-to-43.3 win was built on advance and mail ballots, which Elections BC reports only at the riding level. So this neighbourhood layer shows election-day voting alone — about 42% of all ballots — and runs a couple of points redder than the certified result.

Each dot is a riding: how much more NDP its advance vote was than its election-day vote. They lean almost entirely one way — advance voters were more NDP in 79 of 93 ridings, by 2.9 points on average. That early-voting cushion is what turned an election-day deficit into a one-seat majority.

The closest seats overall, decided by a school gym's worth of voters:

Method: 2024 results by voting place joined to Elections BC's official 2024 Voting-Area → Voting-Place assignment, so each of ~5,780 voting areas across BC inherits the result of the place where its ballots were counted. Areas sharing a place share a value. These are actual election-day counts attributed to catchments — not modelled estimates.

09 · Locked versus liveThe whole board by competitiveness

20Tossups <5 pts
38Safe+Lean NDP
33Safe+Lean Con

Recolour the province by margin and the contest shrinks again. Of 93 seats, fully 20 were tossups, decided by under five points. Most of the rest never moved. An election that looked province-wide was really fought in twenty places — and a clear majority of them were in the suburbs you just saw.

10 · The arithmeticA one-seat majority

Forty-seven is the floor — half of 93, plus one. The NDP cleared it by exactly nothing: 47 seats. The strongholds are banked and the wall is lost; what's left, the actual majority, is the shortlist of suburban and knife-edge seats the party held by a thread.

These are the must-holds — the NDP's narrowest wins. Lose the closest, Surrey-Guildford, by its 22-vote margin, and the majority is already gone.

Sources & Method

Geometry. 2024 electoral-district boundaries (93 ridings), Elections BC / DataBC, reprojected from BC Albers (EPSG:3005) to WGS-84 and simplified for the web.

Results. 2024 figures are actual counts, aggregated from Elections BC's official results by voting place to the district; the totals reproduce the official outcome exactly (NDP 47 · Con 44 · Green 2). Regional vote-share trends for 2013, 2017 and 2020 are aggregated from Elections BC's by-voting-area results and reported at the regional-bloc level — coarse on purpose, because riding boundaries were redrawn twice over this period (85→87→93 seats) and bloc aggregates absorb that churn.

The neighbourhood layer. Step 8 drops below the riding using Elections BC's official 2024 Voting-Area → Voting-Place assignment: each of ~5,780 voting areas across British Columbia is shaded by the result at the final voting place that served it. Under the post-2020 "first-come, first-served" model votes are reported by voting place, so this is the finest honest geography available — and it covers election-day (final) voting only, about 42% of ballots. Advance and mail votes are reported only at the riding level; because they broke toward the NDP, the neighbourhood map runs roughly two points more Conservative than the certified result. Voting areas served by the same place share a value; figures are actual counts attributed to catchments, not modelled.

Turnout and registered-voter counts are not in the supplied files; "votes" shown are valid ballots cast.
